result: The manuscript provides background on neuronal ceroid lipofuscinoses (NCLs), describing their prevalence (2-4 per 100,000 live births), classification as the most common hereditary pediatric neurodegenerative disease, and characteristic features including lipofuscin accumulation and neurodegeneration. CLN1, the infantile form, presents at 6 months with death by ~5 years.
evaluation: Claims C1-C8 are well-supported by citations to established literature (Nita et al., 2016; Haltia, 2006; Jalanko and Braulke, 2009; Bible et al., 2004; Kielar et al., 2007). These are background claims establishing the disease context and are appropriately referenced.

result: The manuscript establishes that CLN1 disease is caused by mutations in PPT1, a depalmitoylating enzyme. Protein palmitoylation is described as a crucial, reversible post-translational modification regulating protein trafficking and function, particularly in neurons. PPT1 localizes to synaptic compartments, and many synaptic proteins including PSD-95 and NMDAR subunits undergo palmitoylation.
evaluation: Claims C9-C17 provide well-established background on PPT1 function and protein palmitoylation, supported by extensive citations (Camp and Hofmann, 1993; Lu and Hofmann, 2006; Hayashi et al., 2005, 2009; Fukata et al., 2006; Kang et al., 2008). These are foundational claims for the study's rationale.

result: The manuscript describes NMDARs as voltage-dependent glutamate-gated ion channels that undergo developmental regulation. GluN2B-containing NMDARs are expressed neonatally with prolonged decay kinetics, and are replaced by GluN2A-containing receptors in response to experience-dependent activity. This switch is mediated by scaffolding proteins SAP102 and PSD-95. PSD-95, GluN2B, and GluN2A all undergo palmitoylation.
evaluation: Claims C18-C24 provide essential background on NMDAR biology and the developmental GluN2B-to-GluN2A switch, well-supported by citations (Cull-Candy et al., 2001; van Zundert et al., 2004; Lau and Zukin, 2007; Paoletti et al., 2013; Sans et al., 2000; Elias et al., 2008). This establishes the biological context for the study's findings.

result: Lipofuscin (autofluorescent lipopigments, ALs) accumulates in Ppt1-/- visual cortex starting at P14 (shortly after eye-opening), earlier than previously reported. ALs accumulated rapidly through the critical period and plateaued by P60. The pattern suggests correlation between neuronal activation and AL accumulation.
evaluation: Claims C25, C31, C32, C80, C81 are supported by data in Figure 1A-C and Supplementary file 1, showing temporal progression of AL accumulation. The finding of earlier AL accumulation (P14 vs. 3-6 months previously reported) is appropriately compared to prior work (Gupta et al., 2001; Blom et al., 2013). Statistical significance is shown at multiple time points.

result: The developmental NMDAR subunit switch from GluN2B to GluN2A is stagnated in Ppt1-/- mice. Biochemical analysis shows GluN2A levels in synaptosomes were significantly lower in Ppt1-/- than WT at P33, P42, and P60, while GluN2B levels were comparable. The GluN2A/GluN2B ratio showed robust decrease in Ppt1-/-. PSD-95 levels were reduced at P33-P60 in Ppt1-/-, while SAP102 remained unchanged. PPT1 expression in synaptosomes increases with age, peaking between P33-P60.
evaluation: Claims C26, C33-C37, C82-C86 are well-supported by biochemical data in Figure 2A-E showing selective reduction in GluN2A and PSD-95 in Ppt1-/- synaptosomes at specific developmental time points (P33-P60). Statistical significance is demonstrated (p<0.05, p<0.01). The temporal correlation between PPT1 expression and the observed deficits strengthens the findings. Sample sizes are adequate (n=4 animals/group with technical replicates).

result: Ppt1-/- neurons exhibit immature evoked NMDAR currents in vivo. Electrophysiological recordings at P42 show decreased fast component and increased slow component of NMDAR-EPSCs, increased weighted decay time (τw), and longer rise time in Ppt1-/- compared to WT. Ro 25-6981 (GluN2B antagonist) treatment decreased τw in both genotypes with no significant difference between them.
evaluation: Claims C27, C38-C42, C87-C89 are supported by electrophysiology data in Figure 3A-E. The findings show functionally immature NMDAR phenotype with appropriate statistical analysis (t-tests, two-way ANOVA). The unexpected lack of differential Ro 25-6981 sensitivity is discussed in context of triheteromeric NMDARs (C89, C133), which is a reasonable interpretation. Sample sizes are adequate (n=8 cells from 4-5 mice per group).

result: Dendritic spine morphology is immature in Ppt1-/- visual cortex at P33. In vivo analysis using in utero electroporation shows Ppt1-/- spines were longer, less voluminous, with reduced spine head volume compared to WT. Dendritic spine density was significantly increased in Ppt1-/- neurons.
evaluation: Claims C43-C45, C90-C92 are supported by morphological data in Figure 4C-F using semi-automated Imaris analysis. Statistical significance is demonstrated (p<0.05, p<0.01, p<0.001). The findings are consistent with immature spine phenotype. Sample sizes appear adequate (n=3-4 cells/animal, 3 animals/group), though the number of animals is modest.

result: The biochemical and morphological phenotypes observed in vivo are recapitulated in cultured Ppt1-/- neurons. At DIV18, GluN2A, PSD-95, and GluN2A/GluN2B ratio showed reductions in Ppt1-/- compared to WT. Dendritic spine analysis at DIV15 and DIV20 showed longer spines, reduced volume, and increased density in Ppt1-/- neurons.
evaluation: Claims C46-C51, C93 are supported by in vitro data in Figures 5B-D and 6B-K. The recapitulation of in vivo phenotypes in culture strengthens the findings and provides a system for mechanistic studies. Statistical significance is shown with appropriate tests. Large spine numbers analyzed (WT=21,514 spines at DIV15; Ppt1-/-=18,013 spines) provide robust statistical power for morphological analysis.

result: Dissociated Ppt1-/- cultured neurons show extrasynaptic, diffuse calcium influxes. Calcium imaging with GCaMP3 revealed that WT neurons exhibited compartmentalized calcium signals restricted to individual spines, while Ppt1-/- neurons demonstrated diffuse calcium influxes spreading through dendritic shafts. Ppt1-/- showed increased area under curve (AUC), calcium diffusion distance, and synchrony. Ro 25-6981 had minimal effect on WT but rescued calcium dynamics in Ppt1-/- to WT levels.
evaluation: Claims C28, C52-C58, C94-C97 are supported by calcium imaging data in Figure 7A-I with Videos 1-4. The findings demonstrate functional consequences of altered NMDAR composition. Statistical significance is shown (p<0.001). Sample sizes are adequate (n=185 synaptic sites for WT, n=131 for Ppt1-/-, from 3 neurons/group). The rescue by Ro 25-6981 specifically in Ppt1-/- neurons supports the role of GluN2B-containing receptors.

result: Ppt1-/- neurons show enhanced vulnerability to NMDA-induced excitotoxicity. Cell viability assays showed that 10 μM NMDA significantly reduced viability in Ppt1-/- but not WT neurons. At 100 μM NMDA, Ppt1-/- viability was reduced by 58% compared to 35% in WT. This is consistent with the predominance of extrasynaptic GluN2B-containing receptors that trigger pro-apoptotic pathways.
evaluation: Claims C59, C60, C102-C105, C117-C119 are supported by cell viability data in Figure 8B showing dose-dependent differential vulnerability. Statistical significance is demonstrated (p=0.046 at 10 μM, p=0.0043 at 100 μM). The findings are consistent with prior work (Finn et al., 2013) and the calcium imaging results. Sample size is adequate (n=4 independent experiments in duplicate).

result: Palmitoylation inhibitors rescue enhanced vulnerability to excitotoxicity in Ppt1-/- neurons. 77% of cultured Ppt1-/- neurons accumulate ALs spontaneously at DIV18-20. Treatment with 2-bromopalmitate (2-BP) or cerulenin reduced AL-positive neurons, AL area, and normalized lysosomal size. Pretreatment with these inhibitors improved Ppt1-/- cell viability to WT levels following NMDA exposure.
evaluation: Claims C61-C64 are supported by data in Figure 9A-F showing that palmitoylation inhibitors reduce AL accumulation and rescue excitotoxicity vulnerability. Statistical significance is demonstrated with two-way ANOVA and Tukey's post-hoc test. Sample sizes are adequate (n=3-4 independent experiments, 7-10 neurons/group for imaging). This is a key therapeutic finding.

result: Palmitoylation inhibitor treatment improves pathological calcium dynamics in Ppt1-/- neurons. Treatment with 2-BP or cerulenin decreased AUC of calcium transients in Ppt1-/- neurons nearly to WT levels. Calcium diffusion distance was similarly improved. Calcium transient frequency was higher in Ppt1-/- than WT but lowest in inhibitor-treated Ppt1-/- neurons.
evaluation: Claims C65, C66, C135 are supported by calcium imaging data in Figure 10A-D with Videos 5-7. Statistical significance is shown with one-way ANOVA and Tukey's post-hoc test. The functional rescue of calcium dynamics by palmitoylation inhibitors supports the mechanistic link between hyperpalmitoylation and the observed phenotypes. Sample sizes are adequate (n=82-185 synaptic sites from 3-4 neurons/group).

result: Ppt1-/- neurons demonstrate hyperpalmitoylation of GluN2B and Fyn kinase. APEGS assay showed that PSD-95 palmitoylation was comparable between WT and Ppt1-/-, suggesting PSD-95 is not a PPT1 substrate. Total Fyn levels were increased in Ppt1-/- and both 2-BP and cerulenin reduced Fyn palmitoylation. Total GluN2B levels were comparable at baseline, but both inhibitors corrected GluN2B hyperpalmitoylation in Ppt1-/- neurons. Fyn is a palmitoylated kinase that phosphorylates GluN2B, affecting its surface stabilization.
evaluation: Claims C29, C67-C72, C110-C112, C123-C126 are supported by APEGS assay data in Figure 11A-I. The finding that PSD-95 palmitoylation is unchanged (C67) is consistent with recent literature (Yokoi et al., 2016, C123). The hyperpalmitoylation of Fyn and GluN2B provides a mechanistic explanation for the observed phenotypes. Statistical significance is shown with two-way ANOVA. Sample sizes are adequate (n=2-4 independent experiments). The differential sensitivity of Fyn vs. GluN2B to inhibitors is noted and discussed.

result: GluN2A shows complex responses to palmitoylation inhibitor treatment in Ppt1-/- neurons. Total GluN2A levels were decreased in Ppt1-/- compared to WT at baseline. GluN2A palmitoylation state was unchanged between genotypes at baseline, suggesting PPT1 is not directly involved in GluN2A depalmitoylation. However, 2-BP treatment in Ppt1-/- neurons robustly increased both total GluN2A levels and palmitoylation state. Cerulenin had more modest effects.
evaluation: Claims C73-C76 are supported by data in Figure 11J-L, but the interpretation is complex and potentially indirect. The authors acknowledge that the increase in GluN2A with 2-BP treatment may reflect correction of upstream defects (e.g., Fyn hyperpalmitoylation) rather than direct effects on GluN2A. The differential effects of 2-BP vs. cerulenin are not fully explained. While the data are clear, the mechanistic interpretation requires further validation.

result: PPT1 plays a critical role in postsynapse maturation by facilitating the GluN2 subunit switch and proteostasis of palmitoylated proteins. The incorporation of GluN2A is experience-dependent, and PPT1 deficiency results in selective degeneration of sensory cortices. PPT1 expression is developmentally regulated and may mediate the switching phenomenon. Multiple signaling pathways (reelin, Wnt-5a, mGluR5) that regulate the GluN2 switch are themselves regulated by palmitoylation.
evaluation: Claims C30, C106-C108, C113-C115 represent the main conclusions of the study, integrating the experimental findings with established literature. The conclusion that PPT1 facilitates postsynapse maturation is well-supported by the convergent evidence from biochemistry, electrophysiology, morphology, calcium imaging, and rescue experiments. The discussion appropriately places findings in context of experience-dependent plasticity and multiple signaling pathways.

result: The rodent visual cortex undergoes well-characterized, timed experience-dependent plasticity. In mice, P11 and P14 are before and after eye opening, respectively. The critical period peaks at P28 and closes from P33-P42. The electroretinogram (ERG) is unaltered at 4 months in Ppt1-/- mice, allowing study of cortical changes.
evaluation: Claims C77-C79, C132 provide methodological justification for using the visual cortex as a model system. These are well-established facts supported by extensive literature (Bear et al., 1990; Gordon and Stryker, 1996; Hensch et al., 1998; Lei et al., 2006). The choice of time points is appropriate for studying developmental plasticity.

result: The manuscript discusses broader implications for neurodegenerative diseases. GluN2B activity enhances filopodial formation, and GluN2B hyperpalmitoylation stabilizes receptors at the cell surface. GAP43 palmitoylation regulates filopodial formation. PSD-95 palmitoylation facilitates spine maturation. GluN2B and Fyn are implicated in Alzheimer's disease, with Fyn in clinical trials. AMPAR and GABAR palmitoylation are implicated in seizures. APP and huntingtin palmitoylation are implicated in Alzheimer's and Huntington's diseases.
evaluation: Claims C98-C101, C127-C131 discuss implications and connections to other diseases, appropriately supported by citations (Henle et al., 2012; Mattison et al., 2012; Kutzleb et al., 1998; Paoletti et al., 2013; Nygaard et al., 2014, 2015; Kaufman et al., 2015; Itoh et al., 2018; Huang et al., 2004; Bhattacharyya et al., 2013). These provide important context for the broader significance of the findings.

result: The manuscript discusses additional context and prior work on CLN1 and NMDARs. Later-onset NCL patients show enlarged VEP prior to degeneration. PPT1 localizes to synapses and influences presynaptic proteins. Presynaptic vesicle pool size is depleted in Ppt1-/- neurons. Cortical neurons predominantly express triheteromeric NMDARs. Extrasynaptic NMDARs remain ifenprodil-sensitive even at maturity.
evaluation: Claims C116, C120-C122, C133-C134 provide additional context from prior literature, appropriately cited (Pampiglione and Harden, 1977; Kim et al., 2008; Virmani et al., 2005; Sheng et al., 1994; Thomas et al., 2006). These help interpret the current findings and explain apparent discrepancies (e.g., Ro 25-6981 sensitivity).
